doc.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Maynard Ferguson and Dizzy's big band
title: Melba Liston as musical director
summary: Melba Liston was Dizzy's musical director and arranger and was treated with respect.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: You were talking about the circumstances that led you to leave the Ferguson band and to go on to your assignment with Dizzy. We talked about that band. In that band, is that your first relationship with Melba Liston?
Yes it was. I didn’t know that she was as heavy musically as she was. I got in that band. I learned it real fast. Musically, she was heavy.
How significant was she to that band? What was her role in that?
She was the musical director. Over all those guys that were there, she was the musical director.
Not just – not in name only, but in substance.

She was the one that was the main arranger in the band. When we had the World of Trombones, the principal trombone player was a woman. She was automatically the musical director, because we all aspired to the things that she could do, Janice Robinson. Melba was the same way. She played really good, and she wrote music that weighs as much as this building. That’s some of the heaviest music I ever heard. It was heavy. The men’s arrangements would sound little peep, peep, peep, around her.
Were there politics around that? Was it resented? Was it accepted? How was she treated?
Dizzy treated her with a hell of a lot of respect. So everybody else had to.

Yeah, they had to. Dizzy wasn’t the guy that would put up with any kind of foolishness. It was all music for him. He was one of the few bandleaders that really was so deeply steeped in music. A lot of the bandleaders didn’t really have much of a knowledge of what they were doing. They were doing what they did, but they didn’t really know that much about it. But they didn’t let the people know that.
